dependency_coverage.name: ite
dependency_coverage.meaning: The if-then-else operator selecting one of two values according to a decidable proposition.
dependency_coverage.effect_on_target: Defines the real indicator I(b) to be 1 when b is true and 0 otherwise.

binders: A proof that p <= 1, so mathematically p lies in the closed interval [0,1].
hypotheses: The only substantive side condition is 0 <= p <= 1; nonnegativity is carried by the type of p and the upper bound is explicit.
No sign or nonzero condition is imposed on lambda.
conclusions: Under the Boolean Bernoulli law that assigns probability p to true and 1-p to false, the integral of b ↦ exp(lambda * I(b)) equals 1 + (exp(lambda) - 1)p, where I(true)=1 and I(false)=0.
The exact expression 1 + (exp(lambda) - 1)p is at most exp((exp(lambda) - 1)p).
mathematical_definitions: I(b) = 1 if b is true and I(b) = 0 if b is false.
The Boolean Bernoulli distribution has mass p at true and mass 1-p at false.
The first integral is therefore the exponential moment E[exp(lambda I(B))] = (1-p) + p exp(lambda) = 1 + (exp(lambda)-1)p.
The second conjunct is the standard inequality 1+x <= exp(x) applied to x = (exp(lambda)-1)p.
translation.proposition_plain_english: For every Bernoulli success parameter p in [0,1] and every real lambda, the exponential moment of the associated 0/1 Boolean outcome is exactly 1 + (e^lambda - 1)p, and this quantity is at most exp((e^lambda - 1)p).

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The probability law is the canonical two-point Boolean Bernoulli law; there is no arbitrary sample space, random-variable function, family, or independence assumption in this proposition.
The parameter p includes both endpoints 0 and 1.
Lambda ranges over all real numbers, including negative values and zero.

The integral has no explicit integrability hypothesis, but its domain is finite and the integrand takes only the two finite values 1 and exp(lambda), so under the ordinary integral meaning it is automatically integrable.
At p=0, both conjuncts reduce to 1=1 and 1<=1; at lambda=0 the same happens for every p. These are valid boundary cases rather than impossible hypotheses.
The exact identity is nontrivial for interior p and nonzero lambda, so the universally quantified proposition is not vacuous.
The upper bound may be loose, but its direction is fixed and it follows for every real value of (exp(lambda)-1)p.
ambiguities: D011 exposes the integral only through an opaque wrapped projection, so the dossier does not reveal its exact convention on nonintegrable functions. This does not affect the displayed finite Boolean integrand under the intended Bochner/Lebesgue interpretation because it is bounded and integrable.
